Photograph taken from very high above, camera pointing straight down at the ground, no horizon and no sky, the earth laid flat like a map in a tall vertical frame. One long pale concrete boundary wall crosses the whole frame from left edge to right edge just below the middle, ruler-straight and casting almost no shadow. Above the wall: a private gated compound of a dozen identical white flat-roofed villas set in a neat grid, each with its own rectangular swimming pool of bright turquoise water, clipped emerald lawns, a single curving driveway, no cars moving, no people anywhere, not a ripple on any pool. Below the wall, packed tight against its base without a single metre of gap: a crowded settlement of improvised shelters roofed in faded blue, grey and rust-coloured tarpaulin and corrugated sheet, narrow dirt lanes, washing strung between roofs, thin threads of grey smoke from cooking fires drifting sideways, people reduced to tiny specks of colour. Even, shadowless light from a thick white overcast, everything sharp from corner to corner, large-format documentary detail, dusty ochre, khaki and ash tones everywhere except the repeated hard blue rectangles of the pools. Calm, still and almost geometric, a composition that first reads as an abstract quilt of shapes and only then as two worlds divided. No text, no signs, no lettering, no logos anywhere. Thanks.

A vertical snapshot taken at night inside the private dining saloon of a vast luxury yacht, the kind of photo someone takes with a cheap point-and-shoot and its built-in flash fired straight ahead. The camera stands at the head of a very long banquet table at seated eye height and looks down its full length toward the dark end of the room. The table is still set for a feast that finished years ago: crumpled white linen gone grey, rows of champagne coupes and tall flutes coated in a fur of pale dust, a silver platter holding a shallow puddle and a few rounded lumps where an ice swan once stood, half-eaten towers of fruit dried to brown husks, a toppled candelabra, napkins dropped on the carpet. Gilded chairs with crimson velvet seats are shoved back at odd angles and one lies on its side, as if the whole party stood up at once and walked out. The flash blasts the foreground in flat bright white, makes the gold leaf and crystal glare, and throws hard black shadows of the chairs and glasses onto the lacquered walls; everything past the middle of the table falls off fast into murk. Behind the far end, a wall of floor-to-ceiling glass shows only pitch-black water and sky, broken by three or four small orange fires burning along a distant shoreline. Saturated, slightly cheap colour: hot reds, brassy gold, sickly green tint in the shadows, a touch of film grain. No people anywhere. Bottles and plates carry no labels, no text, no signs or lettering in the frame. Funny, gaudy and quietly mournful at the same time. Thanks.

A digitally painted illustration with visible soft brushwork and a gouache-like matte finish, portrait frame. A quiet two-lane country road runs straight away from the viewer through a sleepy Nordic housing estate of low timber houses, hedges and a leaning lamp post, at late-afternoon golden hour. In the lower foreground, seen from behind and slightly to one side, a ten-year-old child in a padded jacket sits astride a small bicycle with one foot on the tarmac, shoulders slumped, head tipped toward the empty verge, plainly bored. Halfway down the road a makeshift barrier of planks, painted in faded red and white stripes and propped on trestles, closes the way. Beyond the rooftops, filling the upper half of the frame, a range of colossal windowless data halls and three cooling towers stand dark and cold, their flat grey walls stained by rain, chain-link fences swallowed by waist-high wild grass and birch saplings; nothing moves, no steam, no lights. Camera at the child's eye height, wide lens, deep focus, the vast buildings softened by atmospheric haze so their size reads through distance. Warm honey and amber light rakes across the foreground and throws long shadows up the road, while the distance falls into pale slate blue and lavender. Muted, quiet palette, gentle dust in the air, every surface plain and unmarked. The feeling of a place years after the catastrophe, where the ruins have become ordinary scenery and nobody looks at them any more.

Upright colour photograph made on a large-format view camera standing on its tripod in the exact middle of an empty residential road at midday, lens dead level, both kerbs running away in perfect symmetry towards one vanishing point. Either side, a long unbroken row of matching two-up two-down red-brick terraces with grey slate roofs and paired chimney stacks. Along the pavement, outside each house, that household's whole life has been carried out and left: a floral settee, a child's white cot with the mattress still in it, a fridge-freezer with brown tape across its door, dining chairs stacked upside down, a standard lamp, a telly, swollen cardboard boxes darkened by a passing shower, black bin bags, photographs in frames turned face down on a chest of drawers. The pile is repeated, near identical, at every house down to the far end of the road, as though the bailiffs came for the entire street on one morning. Each front door and downstairs window is sealed with a new sheet of pale unpainted plywood, screwed in tight; house numbers, letterboxes and lettering are all absent. Wet tarmac, no parked cars, no people, no birds. Overcast noon, a blank milky sky giving soft even light with no shadows and no mood. Deep focus, crisp from the kerbstones nearest the lens to the chimney pots at the horizon, fine film grain, quiet natural colour: brick red, wet slate, beige and cream upholstery, the yellow of fresh plywood marching away in rhythm. A neutral, patient, deadpan record, as plain as an estate agent's survey; the stillness carries it.

Vertical portrait shot of a cramped, almost empty council waiting office, seen square-on and dead level from the eye height of someone sitting down, the camera locked off at the far wall so the whole room reads like a stage set built in front of the lens. Exactly on the centre line, one figure sits bolt upright behind a small bare municipal desk of pale laminate on thin steel legs, visible head to shoes beneath the desk. The figure wears a plain charcoal knitted ski mask covering the whole head and neck, a dull grey-green office jacket buttoned to the collar, and dark wool gloves; the gloved hands lie folded one over the other on the empty desktop. On the mask, circling only the wearer's left eye hole, sits a thin crisp white ring, and inside it, at roughly two o'clock, a small red triangle with softened corners pointing downward. The eyes in the holes hold the lens steadily, calm and courteous, as if about to apologise for a very long delay. Behind, a blank wall in washed-out sage, a round white clock whose face has no hands at all, and in one corner a rubber plant in a beige pot, its leaves sagging toward the lino. Beside the desk, a single moulded plastic visitor chair stands empty, turned toward the figure. Speckled grey linoleum underfoot. Everything is sharp from the desk's front edge to the back wall, as through a moderately wide 35mm lens with no distortion. Light is perfectly even and shadowless, a pale overcast glow from ceiling panels with no visible source, leaving skin-pale surfaces, no highlights and no dark corners anywhere. Colours are drained and chalky: putty grey, faded mint, dusty olive, beige, off-white; the one saturated note is the small red triangle. Still, faintly ridiculous and quietly sad, like a polite interview that has already gone badly. No text, signs, posters, labels or lettering anywhere. Thanks.

Vertical frame lifted from a government advice film broadcast on a 1970s television evening, captured on punchy, contrasty 16mm colour reversal stock with heavy visible grain and slightly smeared telecine sharpness. A masked presenter sits squarely in a deep winged armchair covered in tobacco-brown corduroy, centred in a cramped front parlour at night. The wall behind is papered with large repeating hexagons and loops in tangerine, ochre and dark cocoa on a cream ground. A floor lamp with a fringed drum shade stands just off the chair's right ear, its bulb making a warm amber pool over the sitter's shoulders while the room's edges sink into murky umber. Beside the chair, on a low teak occasional table, a bone-china teacup and saucer sit on a crocheted white mat, a curl of steam rising. The presenter's whole head is hidden in a dark navy knitted balaclava with ribbed stitching, only the eyes showing through two holes; encircling the hole of the wearer's left eye is a fine white outline loop, and set within that loop near its upper right, the two o'clock position, a tiny scarlet triangular patch whose three tips are blunted, one tip aimed at the floor. Hands in black leather gloves lie relaxed along both wooden-capped armrests. Framed from the sternum to just above the crown, lens at the sitter's eye height, the gaze fixed directly into camera with the polite, unhurried calm of a man about to talk the nation through its gas bill. Faintly soft focus, saturated oranges and reds against milky faded highlights, inky shadows, a soft darkening falloff around the frame's corners, a speck of dust or two on the emulsion. No writing, captions or lettering anywhere in the picture. Thanks.

Vertical night snapshot taken from barely an arm's length away on a dark porch: a masked visitor's head and shoulders crowd the picture almost edge to edge, caught by one bare speedlight mounted on a bracket right above a short wide lens, so the hard shadow drops straight down behind the neck. The visitor wears an ordinary black wool ski mask, the knit so close and so sharply lit that each twisted strand, bobble and loose hair of yarn reads clearly. Stitched round the eye opening on the wearer's own left (picture right) is a slim white circle; tucked within it, up toward the 2 o'clock position, a tiny crimson triangle, corners rounded off, tip aimed at the ground. Both marks bounce the flash back hot and bright. Behind the mask the gaze holds the lens dead level, steady, unblinking, the patient calm of a well-mannered caller who has already seen how the evening turns out. Low in the corner, a hand in a black glove lifts just above the shoulder line in a modest little wave. Exposure is pushed: the centre of the face glows nearly white, colours run rich and punchy, then the light dies quickly into inky darkness, leaving only a sliver of glossy painted door jamb and the small lit circle of a doorbell floating in the black. Crisp, raw, slightly vignetted, no blur, no writing, numbers or symbols beyond the two marks on the mask. Thanks.

Portrait-format photograph made from the bottom of the shallow end of a long, waterless private pool, aimed straight along its length to the deep end; a 28mm lens held at chest height, so the tiled floor tilts away and climbs toward the far wall, perfect left-right symmetry, deep focus with every tile and window crisp. Years without water: sun-bleached turquoise mosaic crazed with hairline cracks and grimy rings where the waterline used to sit, a heap of dry brown leaves banked around the drain grate, one white resin sun lounger tipped on its side with a leg snapped clean off. Dead centre at the lowest point of the deep end stands a single figure, upright and patient, facing the lens with mild, courteous attention, black leather gloved hands folded behind the back the way a museum guide waits for stragglers. A plain black ribbed-wool ski mask covers the whole head with no skin showing; a slim white circle is stitched around the left eye opening (the wearer's left), and inside that circle, toward its upper right at roughly the two o'clock position, sits a small downward-pointing red triangle with softened corners. Charcoal wool overcoat fastened high, grey slacks, plain shoes. Rising over the pool's edge and filling the top of the frame, the abandoned villa: flaking cream plaster, shutters closed, an empty terrace with one withered potted palm. Even white overcast sky, soft light with no shadows. Chalky, faded colours of bone, pale aqua, ash and leaf-brown, the red triangle the only bright note. Utterly still, formal, quietly ridiculous. No water, nobody else, no lettering, numbers or depth markers anywhere.

Upright portrait seascape at blue hour, some twenty minutes after the sun has gone, shot from a tripod set low beside a sheltered bay at high tide so no rocks or sand intrude. A three-minute exposure has ironed the water into a single seamless pane of dusky steel blue, occupying just the bottom fifth of the picture and softly echoing the sky above it. Along that low, dead-level horizon runs a hairline of far-off coast, a flat charcoal strip with no visible detail, and on it one tiny warm glow, like a porch lamp miles away, which drops a faint thread of gold down across the still water. Above, nothing but sky: an enormous, perfectly smooth gradient that starts as deep indigo near the top edge, eases through royal blue and soft lavender, and ends in a narrow, gentle peach glow resting on the coastline. Cloudless, birdless, no boats, no stars, no lens flare; the upper and central areas stay completely empty and calm, ready to hold a mark added later. Standard focal length, everything sharp, low contrast, clean shadows, a cool hushed palette broken by that single ember of warmth. The mood is the first peaceful dusk after a long disaster: quiet, unhurried, faintly hopeful. Keep it wordless, with no writing, symbols or printed marks on anything.

A single paused frame from a worn home-video tape recorded on a family camcorder in about 1998, cropped tall: a narrow back garden behind a red-brick British terraced house on a hot afternoon, patchy yellowing lawn, a wooden fence with a neighbour's washing line beyond it, and a cheap plastic oscillating sprinkler throwing a glittering fan of water across the grass. Two children, a girl of about seven in a faded pink swimsuit and a younger boy in baggy blue swim shorts, are caught mid-leap through the spray with arms flung out, mouths open in shrieking laughter, wet hair stuck to their foreheads. A child's bike lies on its side on the lawn by a paddling pool, and at the near edge of frame a parent's bare forearm and hand reach in, slightly blurred, as if pointing them out. The camera is held at an adult's waist height, wobbling and tilted a few degrees off level, the focus hunting so everything is gently soft. The look is analogue consumer video: low resolution, smeared fine detail, a faint horizontal smudge where the reds and pinks bleed past their edges, lifted milky blacks, blown-out white sky, slightly muted greens and warm yellow cast, a soft halo of glare around the water droplets, fine tape noise. Ordinary, unposed, a little clumsy, plainly joyful. No text, numbers, date stamp or on-screen markings anywhere in the image. Thanks.

Vertical family snapshot from about 2002, shot on a cheap silver compact digital camera with a low-resolution CCD sensor, its tiny pop-up flash firing straight at the table: a crowded terraced-house lounge at night during a kid's sixth birthday. Framed tight and lopsided, horizon leaning to the right, the birthday girl sits low in the frame with a gappy grin and a crooked paper crown, lips pursed at five wobbling candles on a supermarket sponge cake smeared with blue icing. Behind her a scrum of cousins, a dad in a football shirt and a nan in a cardigan whoop with arms in the air; one lad sticks his tongue out, one aunt stares back with glowing red pupils. The flash flattens every face into bright shiny skin and blown-out white napkins, casts a hard black halo-shadow on the woodchip wallpaper, then dies within a couple of metres so the back of the room drops into a murky tangerine haze from a single standard lamp. Clutter crammed into the corners: helium balloons drifting against the artex ceiling, a party-ring biscuit plate, paper cups of fizzy pop, ripped gift wrap over a loud paisley carpet. Colour cranked and garish, warm-yellow cast, greenish noise blotches in the shadows, crunchy compression smearing the dark edges, a little soft from a plastic lens. Chaotic, loud, joyful. Leave the frame free of writing, date stamps, numbers or logos. Thanks.

A snapshot from a 1998 family day trip to the English coast, the sort of print that sat in a shoebox for twenty years and was scanned slightly skewed: shot with a single-use plastic film camera, fixed focus, one click of the winding wheel per frame. A gusty bright noon on a steep bank of grey pebbles. Front and centre a beaming grandad, shirt untucked, trouser legs turned up to the shins, pale bony ankles in the stones, punches a ninety-nine-style whippy cone up at the sky as if he has just won the cup final, white cream sliding down over his knuckles. Two little ones at his knees, a girl in a pink anorak with her hood whipped back and a boy in a football shirt, swing sand-pails and squint, one doubled over laughing; a nan perched on a stripy deckchair behind them, hand clamped on her hat. Behind the family a ragged line of candy-striped canvas breaks in faded red, blue and yellow strains against the wind on wooden stakes, and past them a slate-green sea chops under a sky bleached almost white. Held at chest height by an aunt, the whole frame leaning a touch to the left, heads nearly clipped at the top, a smudge of out-of-focus pink skin just intruding at the lower right edge. Flat overhead sunlight, a stop too bright, so the highlights flare and the pebbles go chalky; skin glows warm butter-yellow while sky and water drift towards cool aqua; shadows muddy with a faint green tint. The plastic lens keeps nothing truly crisp, softness growing towards the edges, the four corners sinking into dusky falloff, a thin rainbow fringe on bright edges, gritty consumer-film grain, low washed contrast. Unposed and mid-shout, imperfect and loved. The picture carries no writing of any kind: clean corners without printed numbers, plain clothing, unbranded cones and pails, nothing lettered on the windbreaks. Thanks.

Camera pressed into the turf at the foot of a smooth rolling hill, tilted upward, so tall blades of vivid emerald grass frame the bottom of the tall portrait picture, the closest ones razor sharp and beaded with dew, the farthest melting into soft green blur. Halfway up the slope a young family sprawls on a red-and-white checked rug beside a wicker basket: a mum, a dad and a little girl in crisp white and pale pastel clothes, all three mid-laugh with heads tipped back, while their golden retriever hangs in the air above them in a joyful leap, ears flapping, paws tucked. Big oily-sheened soap bubbles float everywhere, a couple of them huge and right against the lens, their skins swirling with pink, turquoise and gold. Over everything a deep, almost unreal cobalt sky, darker at the top, dotted with a few neat puffy white clouds, and a blazing noon sun peeking into one top corner, its star-shaped glare spilling a slanting trail of pale hexagonal flare rings down across the bubbles. The feel of a glossy mid-2000s advertising stock photo promising a bright tomorrow: wide-angle, high clean daylight, saturated and polished, slight glow blooming off the whites, firm contrast, not a speck of dirt, colours kept to sky blue, lawn green, bright white and sunny yellow. The picture carries no words, signs or printed marks of any kind. Thanks.

A single frame lifted from an old family tape, filmed one July evening around 2001 and dubbed to disc years later: soft and smeary, low in detail, colours bleeding a fraction past their edges, a fizz of grain in the darker areas. The setting is the turning circle at the end of a council-house close, rows of pebble-dashed semis with low brick walls and wheelie bins, the road surface still warm. A loose kickabout is under way, goals marked by two heaps of dumped sweatshirts, a mix of lanky teenagers and small kids in baggy shorts and plain knock-off football tops chasing a scuffed ball, while one boy of about twelve peels away after scoring, both arms stretched out like wings, shouting at the sky. Off to the side a woman in her fifties in a cardigan and slippers stands on her front step cradling a mug of tea, grinning at them. Seen from the far end of the street, zoomed all the way in so the houses compress into a flat stacked backdrop and the players overlap, the framing slightly tilted and handheld, as if a dad held it up from behind his garden gate. The sun sits low right behind the game: hair and shoulders outlined in glowing gold, a broad hazy flare smeared across the upper half, the sky blown to a milky cream that eats into the rooftops, and long skinny shadows running down the tarmac towards us. Shadows are grey and murky rather than black, reds slightly overcooked, the whole picture steeped in apricot, honey and washed-out rose. Candid, unposed, nobody aware of the lens: the feeling that the holidays have weeks left and it will never get dark. The image is clean of any writing, overlay, timecode or emblem; tops are blank and house numbers too blurry to read. Thanks.

A school picture-day portrait from around 2003, the kind of glossy print that came home in a cardboard folder with a sheet of wallet-sized copies. A figure in a plain black knitted balaclava sits upright on a low photographer's stool, shoulders turned slightly to one side the way pupils were always angled, chin a touch down, the masked face turned dead to the lens with calm, polite stillness. The balaclava has no eye, nose or mouth holes, so no skin shows anywhere; a large white ring is stitched round the whole face, and one small red triangle with rounded corners, pointing down, sits high inside the ring on the right-hand side of the picture. Black woollen gloves rest one over the other on its knee, and it wears a tidy navy V-neck school jumper over a white collared shirt, collar slightly crooked. Behind it hangs the familiar mottled canvas backdrop, cloudy grey-blue darkening toward the edges, softly out of focus. The light is flat and forgiving: a big soft main light from front-left and a gentle fill, so the mask, ring and triangle are evenly lit with almost no shadow, plus a faint hair light rimming the top of the head. Head-and-shoulders crop, centred, medium telephoto compression, camera at chest height. The colour is that slightly too-smooth, warm-skewed minilab print of the era: lifted blacks, creamy highlights, a gentle magenta-blue cast, fine grain and the soft sheen of photo paper. Ordinary, wholesome, and very wrong. The print is clean: no writing, digits, name plates or stamps.

A still lifted from somebody's family videotape, late 1990s, a birthday do in a cramped front room filmed by an uncle with a palm-sized tape camcorder. Twisted paper streamers in red, green and yellow droop from the light fitting, a balloon has drifted against the woodchip wallpaper, and a folding table under a plastic party cloth holds sausage rolls on a foil tray, a bowl of crisps, a hedgehog of cheese-and-pineapple sticks stuck in half a grapefruit, a wobbly orange jelly and paper cups. Behind the table the relatives are dancing to something on the stereo, cardigans and loud patterned shirts swinging, their arms and faces dragged into soft combed smears by the motion; a grandad in a paper crown is laughing at the back. Mid shot, the lens wide and slightly bowed at the frame edges. Closest to camera, filling the lower middle of the portrait frame, stands one extra guest in a plain dark-grey knitted ski mask and plain knitted gloves, nothing of them uncovered. The balaclava has no eye, nose or mouth holes, so no skin shows anywhere; a large white ring is stitched round the whole face, and one small red triangle with rounded corners, pointing down, sits high inside the ring on the right-hand side of the picture. One gloved hand holds a sagging paper plate with a single sausage roll on it. They have turned their head to meet the camcorder dead on, perfectly still, polite, patient, as though about to say thank you for having me. Nobody behind them has clocked it. The camcorder's built-in lamp blasts a flat, frontal, shadowless pool of white light onto the masked head and shoulders so the knit texture, the white ring and the red triangle are crisp and evenly lit, while the room behind drops off into warm tungsten amber and muddy brown with a soft dark vignette. Tape-era texture: colours soft and smeared sideways past their edges, a red-orange glow bleeding off the foil and the bright cups, shadows noisy and crawling with grain, blacks milky and lifted, a slight handheld tilt. Warm, daft, happy and homely, with one guest who does not belong. The picture carries no words, digits, date overlay or symbols of any kind.

A night photo from a travelling funfair around 2003, snapped on a cheap pocket digital camera with its built-in xenon flash going off at point-blank range, the sort of hasty holiday shot that later turns up in a happy throwback slideshow. Centre of the frame, seen from about the waist up and from slightly beneath, stands a figure in a plain dark-navy knitted ski mask and thick woollen gloves, body square to the lens, the masked face turned straight out with mild, patient politeness. The balaclava has no eye, nose or mouth holes, so no skin shows anywhere; a large white ring is stitched round the whole face, and one small red triangle with rounded corners, pointing down, sits high inside the ring on the right-hand side of the picture. The whole face area is evenly lit, sharp and clear. In one gloved hand it holds a huge cloud of bubblegum-pink candyfloss on a paper stick; from the other hangs a tied clear plastic bag of water with a single orange goldfish won at a hook-a-duck stall. The flash makes the figure bright, flat and a little overexposed, with a hard dark shadow tucked close behind it, while everything further back falls away into night: the waltzer cars and the light-bulb arches of the rides are only long wobbly trails of magenta, lime, gold and electric blue where the slow shutter dragged them during a small hand shake, floating in a deep black sky speckled with coloured digital noise. Over-saturated early sensor colour, a cool blue tint on the flash-lit wool, purple fringing around the brightest lamps, mild softness at the edges, frame leaning a few degrees. Canopies and booths are plain blank fabric, and nothing in the image carries letters, numbers, signs or symbols. Thanks.

Vertical frame of a deserted recreation ground at the very end of a hot summer day, roughly 1999: knee-high meadow grass gone gold and feathery fills the bottom third, and half hidden in it lies a small kid's BMX dropped on its side, handlebars twisted, one pedal pointing at the sky. Behind it the field runs flat to a thin dark strip of oak trees and a single wooden bench, tiny and far away, and that low horizon sits well below the middle of the picture. The upper half is pure open sky, a smooth wash that starts as warm peach just above the trees and cools upward into a faded powder blue, empty of clouds, birds, wires and aircraft. The camera is a family handycam propped on a garden wall at adult eye level, left recording and untouched, framed straight and level, focus drifting slightly soft. The image has the gentle smeary quality of a tape transfer from a home video compilation: colours slightly bleached and rosy, the peach glowing and bleeding a touch into the tree line, a fine fizz of chroma speckle in the darkening grass, faint horizontal wobble near the bottom edge, highlights soft and milky. Mood: hushed, warm and a little heartbreaking, the moment after the last kid has been shouted home and the tape keeps rolling over nothing. The picture is clean of any writing, numbers, overlays or graphics.

Vertical frame shot from ground level, the lens nestled low among blades of grass and tilted steeply upward. Tall slender blades of vivid lime-green grass rise into the frame from the bottom and both edges, each blade unnaturally smooth and glossy as if lacquered, with sunlit yellow-lime tips, deep emerald shadows at their bases and tiny round dew droplets clinging along their edges, each droplet holding its own pinpoint of light. Above them a flawless saturated cyan sky deepens to rich royal blue at the very top, crossed by a few thin, feathery white cloud wisps. Large transparent soap bubbles float upward through the frame at different heights and sizes, their thin skins swirling with faint rainbow film of magenta, gold and teal, each topped by a crisp white crescent highlight from the high overhead sun and a softer glint on its lower rim. One big bubble in the lower middle of the frame is razor sharp and works like a curved mirror, holding a tiny warped reflection of the bright meadow and sky; the bubbles farther away melt into soft round circles of blurred light. In the upper left corner a gentle white and pale-cyan sun flare blooms with a few faint circular rings trailing diagonally across the sky. Macro lens, very shallow depth of field, crisp high-key midday light, super saturated clean palette of lime, cyan, aqua and pure white, polished and immaculate like a glossy mid-2000s computer desktop background or an upbeat stock photograph about a bright tomorrow, cheerful to the point of feeling slightly too perfect. No people, no text, no lettering, no logos. Thanks.

Tall portrait shot from deep inside a sunny lagoon, the camera low and angled up toward the light through water so clean and turquoise it looks freshly rendered. High overhead the surface is a shimmering silver-white ceiling, and broad shafts of sunshine slant down through it in long diagonal bands that soften and fade before they reach the pale sand. Suspended dead centre, a flawless clear glass sphere about the size of a beach ball hangs weightless: a crisp crescent of white light gleams along its top rim, a gentle cyan glow wraps its underside, and the bright water behind it bends and magnifies as if seen through a lens. Where the beams pass through the sphere they break into a trembling web of light ripples across the sand beneath. Three plump orange goldfish with trailing veil tails glide past on the left, a pair of yellow-and-black banded reef fish dart across to the right, and from a pale coral at the bottom of the frame a thin chain of silver bubbles wobbles upward past the glass toward the sun. The whole scene is glossy, spotless and slightly too perfect, like a desktop aquarium on an early-2000s computer left running in a bright office: saturated aqua, cyan and pure white with warm orange accents, crisp high-definition detail, soft bloom on every highlight, no murk, no debris, no people, no text or lettering anywhere. Thanks.

Looking straight down from directly above onto an unmade bed with a crumpled white duvet, an outfit laid out flat as if someone is planning their Saturday: a red and black checked flannel shirt spread open with its sleeves flung wide, a pair of pale blue skinny jeans torn open at both knees, a thin black velvet choker coiled in a loose loop at the collar, gold-framed aviator sunglasses with mirrored lenses, a pair of scuffed white canvas lace-up trainers placed toe to toe, and a crown of small pink and cream silk flowers resting where a head would be. Beside the clothes, balanced on the duvet, sits a round coconut-shell bowl of deep purple acai with neat rows of banana coins, blueberries, raspberries and a scatter of golden granola, a spoon resting across the rim. Soft early-morning sun pours in from a window on the left, throwing long warm shadows across the fabric creases. The frame is tilted a few degrees off level and slightly crooked, casually snapped on a phone held at arm's length for a camera-roll dump. The colour treatment is a heavy mid-2010s app filter: blacks lifted to a milky charcoal, highlights pushed honey-gold, colours turned up loud so the flannel red and the acai purple almost glow, a faint warm vignette and fine digital grain. No people, no faces, no hands, no writing, labels or logos on anything. Thanks.

A tall portrait photograph of an empty converted warehouse flat on a golden late afternoon, nobody in it, the camera tucked down in one corner of the room at roughly waist height with a slightly wide lens so the old brick walls lean in a little and the ceiling beams run away overhead. Big multi-pane steel-framed industrial windows fill the back wall and pour thick honey-coloured sun across scuffed wide floorboards, with specks of dust drifting through the light. Bare amber filament bulbs dangle on long black cords from the rafters and a loose string of warm fairy lights is looped along the exposed brick. Nearest the lens, a low coffee table made of rough salvaged planks holds a glass preserving jar stuffed with daisies and cornflowers, a second jar glowing with tea lights, a cream mug covered in a tiny repeating curled-moustache pattern, and a stack of record sleeves in plain brown kraft card. Behind it a cracked tan leather sofa with a chunky knitted throw and a small ukulele resting against one arm. A turntable sits on an upturned crate in the midground with its lid up. By the door, a skinny single-speed bicycle with a mint-green frame leans against the brick. One wall is painted matte blackboard black and wiped completely clean, and every other surface stays bare and unprinted, so the edit can lay its own bright captions over it later. The whole frame is graded like a phone snapshot from 2012 run through a faded vintage filter: lifted milky blacks, creamy yellow-beige highlights, slightly washed mint and peach midtones, edges going gently soft and a soft dark vignette in the corners. Hopeful, cosy and a touch smug, the feeling of a cheap first flat when everything was going to work out. Thanks.
"We used to be a country": the 2005 shopping centre

A tall portrait snapshot taken by someone leaning over the brass-and-glass balustrade of the third floor of a huge suburban shopping centre, looking straight down into its central atrium on a busy Saturday afternoon in about 2005. The near edge of the frame is the top rail of that balustrade, caught bright and slightly blown out by the camera's own little flash, a fingerprint smear of glare on the glass panel below it. Beneath, three stacked galleries of shopfronts curve around the void, each one a plain lit window of folded clothes, trainers or homeware under a smooth fascia band painted a single flat colour and left completely blank. At the bottom sits a three-tier marble fountain throwing white plumes into a round pool whose floor glitters with hundreds of copper and silver coins, ringed by big potted palms and slatted wooden benches. A capsule lift with glass walls hangs halfway up its column, a few tiny passengers inside. Further down, a crowded food court of round tables and plastic trays, shoppers as small soft blurs mid-stride with carrier bags swinging, every face too small and smeared to read. Overhead a long barrel-vault skylight pours flat white daylight over everything, bouncing off glossy cream floor tiles and polished chrome. Shot on a cheap early digital compact: slightly soft, a touch of sensor noise in the shadows, highlights that wash out to white, colours a little faded toward warm cream, mint, terracotta and pale blue, horizon a few degrees off level. Every surface is wordless: bare shop fascias, plain carrier bags, unmarked trays and cups. Busy, warm, prosperous, ordinary: the feeling that there was money and somewhere to go. Thanks.

Seen from high above at golden hour, a glossy utopian eco city in the optimistic green-tech style of a 2008 sustainability brochure fills the tall frame: clusters of pearl-white towers with soft rounded curves step upward like stacked petals, each balcony and roof overflowing with ferns, shrubs and young trees; on the rolling lime-green hills beyond, a line of slender white wind turbines spins, their blades smeared with motion; transparent geodesic greenhouse domes shelter palms and catch the light; a sleek white maglev train slides along a looping raised track; a turquoise lagoon, perfectly calm, reflects the whole skyline like a mirror. The surfaces gleam as if freshly polished, colours are juicy and saturated, curved edges carry bright white glints, and a soft cyan sun flare and a few drifting translucent light spheres hang in the upper air. The city is entirely deserted: vacant plazas, an empty train, untouched paths, not a single soul. Near the bottom of the frame, small against all this, a smooth white walkway curves past a glossy railing, and on it one figure stands utterly motionless, facing us head-on with arms hanging loose, wearing a dark charcoal knitted balaclava that encloses the whole head with no holes for eyes, nose or mouth, a large white stitched ring circling the entire face, and high inside that ring on the right side of the picture one small red triangle with rounded corners pointing down; dark gloves, plain dark clothing, not a patch of skin showing. A single rainbow-sheened soap bubble floats still beside its shoulder. At the farthest rim of the sky, low behind the hills, a faint dull-grey haze has begun to seep into the blue. Tall portrait framing, deep focus throughout, warm honey sunlight raking in from the left, a palette of sky blue, lime, white, turquoise and gold broken only by that cold grey smear. Every sign panel, every hull and wall is plain and unmarked, carrying no writing or emblems of any kind. Thanks.

Tall portrait snapshot taken in a festival meadow during the summer of 2016, the sun a hand's width above a treeline and sinking fast. Trampled grass, hay-coloured dust lifting in the backlight, sagging lines of warm bulb lights strung on timber posts above, half of them just flickering on. Tissue confetti in coral, gold and aqua tumbles through the air, frozen mid-drop. All around, a jubilant crowd turned away from us and melted into soft blur: bare shoulders, arms flung up, crochet tops, cut-off denim, braided hair woven with crowns of artificial daisies and peonies, nobody looking back. Exactly in the middle distance, the single crisp thing in the whole picture, a lone figure stands square to the lens, utterly motionless, arms hanging, a gloved fist gripping a burning sparkler that spits a tiny white fizz. Its head is covered by a dark knitted balaclava with no openings for eyes, nose or mouth, so not a speck of skin is visible; a bold white ring is stitched all the way round the face, and inside that ring, up high and toward the viewer's right, sits one little red downward-pointing triangle whose corners are rounded off. Black gloves, plain dark layers, nothing mechanical. Captured at shoulder height on a cheap mid-2010s phone lens, a touch wide, the low sun parked just past the right edge so a huge amber-and-rose flare with polygon ghosts smears across the dancers. Graded like a heavily filtered upload of that year: milky raised shadows, cranked saturation, tangerine highlights, a pink wash, fine grain, a gentle dark vignette. Happy chaos melting everywhere, one rigid sharp silhouette at its centre. Keep the frame free of words, signs, banners and printed marks. Thanks.
Chill guy from the future (mask to fix)

Full-length portrait, camera level with the chest, of one lone figure planted dead centre on a single seamless sweep of pale peach-apricot paper that runs unbroken from floor to top edge, flat as an empty meme template. The figure's head is wrapped in a snug charcoal knitted balaclava that is completely closed, unbroken wool over the brow, the nose bridge and the lips; a broad loop of white stitching rings the entire face; inside that loop, up toward the top on the viewer's right, a little red triangle, corners rounded off, its apex aiming downward. Grey knit gloves, so not a patch of skin is visible. It wears a baggy oversized oatmeal cardigan that drowns the wrists, hanging open over a plain cream tee, loose khaki cargo trousers rumpling over chunky off-white trainers. Body language of total unbothered calm: both gloved fists buried deep in the cardigan pockets, hips cocked so the weight rests on one leg, the other knee soft, shoulders slack and rounded, the masked head leaning a few degrees as though faintly amused by the whole world. Straight-on 50mm look, head to soles in frame, the figure sitting low and compact with generous empty peach space overhead and either side for captions to go on later. Big soft frontal studio light, almost shadowless, just a faint grey shadow pooling under the trainers, matte knit texture readable. Palette of peach, oatmeal, khaki, charcoal and white, with that one red mark as the only accent. The paper sweep stays blank and unmarked, nothing written or printed on it or on the clothes. Thanks.
Lo-fi window seat (triangle on wrong side, to fix)

Tall portrait frame of a snug little bedroom in the small hours, viewed from a few steps back across the room at sitting height, slightly off to one corner. In the window bay, a figure lounges sideways along a wide padded sill, back propped on one wall of the recess, both knees bent up, feet in fluffy socks, the whole body loose and sunk into the cushions like it has nowhere to be. Its head is wrapped completely in a dark navy knitted balaclava, solid wool where eyes, nose and mouth would be, not a sliver of skin showing. A broad loop of bright white yarn is sewn around the full oval of the face, and up near the top of that loop, on the right as we look at it, sits a little red triangle with soft rounded points, its tip aimed downward. Huge padded headphones clamp over the wool. It wears a baggy mustard hoodie with the sleeves pushed down over dark knitted gloves, and both gloved hands cup a fat speckled mug from which a lazy ribbon of steam rises. Its head is tilted back against the glass in pure contentment, angled three-quarters to us. Behind it the window is beaded and streaked with rain, and through the wet pane a far-off skyline of stacked flats and towers glimmers in bubblegum pink, lilac and electric blue, softened into dreamy smears of colour. On the near side of the room: a small wooden desk with a bendy lamp pouring syrupy orange light onto an open notebook and a crooked pile of library books, a leafy monstera in a terracotta pot, a strand of tiny warm bulbs draped along a shelf, a rumpled duvet just catching the edge of frame. Soft hand-drawn animation look, cel-style flat shading with gentle gradients, faint paper grain, glowing halos around each bulb, warm amber indoors meeting cool violet night at the window frame, low contrast and hushed, the cosy calm before a word is said. Nothing written anywhere in the picture: no words, signage, labels or brand marks, and no pets. Thanks.

Tall portrait frame, the final resting screen of an optimistic mid-2000s desktop paradise as dusk arrives. Across only the lowest fifth rises a single smooth grassy mound, rounded like a pillow, its lawn so even it looks polished, glowing electric lime on the sunlit crown and sliding into deep emerald along the side that turns away from the light. Above it opens a colossal unbroken sky, glossy as lacquered glass: rich cyan overhead, softening through bright seawater aqua, then settling into a hushed dusky blue that meets the grass, with one faint pastel shimmer of aurora low along the skyline. Everything above the mound for the top two thirds is empty, smooth gradient sky, a clean resting place left for something to appear later. Five or six clear soap bubbles drift upward and off to the left from behind the crest, each with a bright pane of reflected light and an oily rainbow rim, the highest ones dwindling to pinpricks. Planted dead centre on the crest, tiny in the frame and visible from boots to crown, a solitary person faces straight into the camera with arms resting at the sides: dark zip jacket, dark trousers, knitted dark gloves, and a close-fitting charcoal wool balaclava covering the whole head with no openings for eyes, nose or mouth, so no skin is visible anywhere. A thick white stitched ring outlines the entire face, and high inside that ring, on the right-hand side of the picture, one small red downward-pointing triangle with softly rounded corners. Long-lens view from far off and slightly below, level horizon, the person crisp, a narrow rim of golden evening light along the shoulders, sleek computer-rendered finish with gentle glow and bloom, candy-bright colours muted to a calm hush. Mood: serene, courteous, a held breath at the end of a promise, the quiet after someone says watch this space. No lettering, signs, logos or symbols anywhere in the image. Thanks.
